# Findings & Failure Cases

**Data used for this write-up:** synthetic (labelled) OHLCV data generated by
`src/data_pipeline.generate_synthetic_universe`, because this build
environment's network is restricted to package registries and cannot reach
`query1/query2.finance.yahoo.com`. The synthetic generator is not a plain
random walk — it has volatility clustering (GARCH(1,1)-style), regime
switches, a shared market factor with per-asset betas, and volume that
co-moves with realised volatility — so the numbers below are a genuine
stress-test of the pipeline's methodology, just not a claim about real
ESG/clean-energy stocks. Re-run `python3 main.py` on a machine with normal
internet access (see README "Running on real data") and every number here
regenerates from live prices with zero code changes.

## 1. Predictive metrics (out-of-sample, averaged over 5 walk-forward folds)

| model | RMSE | Directional accuracy | Rank IC |
|---|---|---|---|
| ridge | 0.01287 | 51.4% | **0.0101** |
| naive_drift | 0.01808 | 50.5% | 0.0090 |
| lstm | 0.01288 | 50.0% | 0.0027 |
| gbm | 0.01314 | 49.6% | -0.0063 |
| naive_zero | 0.01287 | — | n/a |

**Failure case #1 — RMSE is a misleading headline metric here.**
`naive_zero` (always predict "no move") has RMSE *tied with the best model*.
That's expected and correct: at daily frequency, the vast majority of a
stock's forward return is unpredictable noise, so a model that predicts
approximately zero every day will always look "fine" on RMSE. This is why
the project design deliberately also reports **rank IC** (does the model's
*ranking* of assets correlate with what actually happened, cross-sectionally)
and **directional accuracy**, and why any single metric on its own would
have been dishonest here.

**Failure case #2 — the ML and DL models did not clearly beat linear/naive
baselines.** Ridge (a straightforward linear baseline) had the best average
rank IC; GBM was net negative; the LSTM was positive but small and noisy. On
this synthetic data, the signal-to-noise ratio in the engineered features is
low enough that added model capacity (trees, recurrent nets) mostly fits
noise rather than finding structure a linear model misses. **This is a
realistic, well-documented phenomenon in daily-frequency equity return
prediction** — it is not a bug in the LSTM or GBM code. The honest
conclusion from this run is "no model showed a robust, reliable edge," not
"pick whichever number happened to be positive this run."

## 2. Fold-by-fold instability (see `outputs/fold_diagnostics.png`)

**Failure case #3 — the signal (such as it is) is not stable across time.**
Rank IC per fold swings from clearly positive (fold 0, all models) to
clearly negative (fold 4, all models simultaneously). All five models move
together across folds — evidence this is being driven by the shared
market/volatility regime in the underlying data, not by anything
model-specific. A model selected on fold-0 performance alone would have
looked great and then failed later; this is exactly why the project uses
**multiple chronological folds** rather than a single train/test split, and
why any real deployment needs regime-awareness (e.g. conditioning on
realised volatility, or accepting that the strategy will have real
drawdown periods and sizing risk accordingly) rather than assuming a
backtested edge is constant.

## 3. Strategy performance: gross vs. net of costs

Daily rebalance, top/bottom-2-of-7 long/short, 5bps commission + 10bps
slippage:

| model | gross Sharpe | net Sharpe | avg daily turnover | net max drawdown |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| naive_drift | 0.48 | **-4.94** | 1.41 | -93.7% |
| gbm | -0.08 | -4.69 | 1.21 | -92.8% |
| ridge | 0.02 | -3.90 | 0.99 | -87.8% |
| lstm | -0.02 | -2.79 | 0.71 | -76.5% |
| naive_zero | -0.06 | -0.07 | 0.00 | -23.1% |

**Failure case #4 — this is the single most important result in the whole
project.** Every model with a nonzero predicted signal loses badly once
realistic transaction costs are applied, even where the *gross* (pre-cost)
Sharpe ratio looked roughly break-even or mildly positive. Daily
rebalancing of a rank-based long/short book on a 7-asset universe produces
turnover near 100–140% *per day* — because the top/bottom-2 ranking flips
around whenever predictions are this noisy — and 15bps round-trip costs on
that much turnover compounds into a devastating annual drag (roughly
15bps × ~250 trading days × ~1.0 turnover ≈ 37% per year, which is almost
exactly what's observed). **A model can pass a predictive-metrics review
and still be a strategy that guarantees ruin once you account for how
often it trades.** This is precisely the class of mistake the target
company's own project description flags (costs/slippage, forward testing)
and precisely the class of mistake a purely "Kaggle-style" backtest (fit
model, report accuracy, stop) would never catch.

## 4. Mitigation: reducing rebalance frequency

Same models, same signal, only difference: **rebalance weekly instead of
daily** (`outputs/strategy_metrics_weekly_rebalance.csv`):

| model | gross Sharpe | net Sharpe | avg daily turnover | net max drawdown |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| lstm | 0.32 | **-0.58** | 0.23 | -44.7% |
| gbm | 0.07 | -1.02 | 0.27 | -47.8% |
| naive_drift | -0.11 | -1.24 | 0.29 | -52.2% |
| ridge | -0.36 | -1.42 | 0.26 | -56.2% |
| naive_zero | -0.06 | -0.07 | 0.00 | -23.1% |

Turnover drops ~5x and every model's net Sharpe improves substantially — the
LSTM in particular goes from deeply negative to only mildly negative and has
the best *gross* Sharpe of any model here (+0.32), suggesting whatever weak
signal it captures decays too fast to survive daily costs but partially
survives weekly rebalancing. **None of these strategies is presented as
"working"** — the honest reading of this whole project is that a simple
rank-based signal on daily-frequency equity returns, built from public price/
volume data alone, does not clear realistic trading costs on this dataset.
That is itself a valid, common, and defensible research finding — most
signals don't work, and knowing *how* to find that out rigorously (rather
than overfitting until something looks good) is the actual skill being
demonstrated.

## 5. What I would try next (and why I didn't do it here)

- **Lower-frequency targets** (weekly/monthly forward returns instead of
  daily) — daily-frequency equity returns are close to the hardest, noisiest
  target in finance; costs also bite less at lower turnover by construction.
- **More assets / broader universe** — 7 assets is small for a
  cross-sectional rank strategy; more names reduces the "coin-flip" quality
  of top/bottom-2 selection.
- **Volatility-scaled position sizing** instead of equal weight, to reduce
  the punishing drawdowns visible above.
- **A no-trade band / hysteresis** (only rebalance a name if its rank moves
  by more than N positions) as a cheaper alternative to periodic
  rebalancing, keeping the model "current" while still controlling turnover.
- **Feature-importance / SHAP analysis on the GBM model** to check whether
  it's learning anything economically sensible or just noise — a natural
  next step once a model shows a real edge worth interrogating.
- **Ensembling models and/or ensembling across folds' predictions** to
  reduce the instability seen in the fold-by-fold IC chart.

I scoped this project to demonstrate the *methodology* (walk-forward, no
look-ahead, realistic costs, DL model, honest evaluation) end-to-end
correctly, rather than iterating until a backtest looked good — iterating
toward a good-looking backtest without a train/validation/test discipline
strict enough to catch it is exactly how look-ahead bias and overfitting
sneak into real quant research.
